extracted.intended_audience: researchers and practitioners in early childhood education / developmental psychology studying children's humour and pictorial expression
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and empirical rubric for collecting, coding, and interpreting 5–6 year-old children's drawings about humour (pictorial humour), including theoretical categorizations (Absurd, Bariaud, McGhee) and qualitative methods (drawing + semi-structured interview + content analysis).

rubrics_metrics.name: Bariaud's / McGhee's four characteristics of pictorial humour
rubrics_metrics.description: These transferring of characteristics are classified as: a) characteristics or displacement of characteristics; b) deformity-exaggeration in size; c) abnormal behaviours or situations; and d) misfortune or misbehaviours.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these four characteristic categories to understand pictorial humour in preschool drawings; examples include exaggerated size, transferred characteristics (human traits on animals), abnormal behaviours, and mishaps/clumsiness. (Original wording from the literature cited: Bariaud (2) and McGhee (20,21).)

rubrics_metrics.name: Absurd Theory categories of humour (Loizou)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Theory of the Absurd consists of three categories: 1) comic gestures/attitudes/voices/words; 2) inconvenient activities; and 3) the use of inconvenient materials.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classify drawn humourous elements by whether they depict comic gestures (facial expressions, voices), inconvenient or inappropriate activities, or use of unexpected/inconvenient materials; this framework helps interpret children's sense of humour as 'absurd'.

rubrics_metrics.name: McGhee's five developmental stages of humour
rubrics_metrics.description: McGhee separates the development of humour into five phases: Phase 1 — infants laugh at attached figures (≈6–15 months); Phase 2 — object substitution/inconsistent behaviours (≈12/15 months–3–5 years); Phase 3 — naming people/objects/body parts in an inconsistent way (≈2–4 years); Phase 4 — conceptual incongruity with subcategories (4a playing with sounds; 4b combining meaningless and real words; 4c distortion of characteristics; 4d giving names related to the opposite sex); Phase 5 — multiple senses/wordplay and adult-like humour (≈6/7 years and later).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analyzing drawings and verbal explanations, map expressed humour to these developmental phases (e.g., object substitution indicates Phase 2; wordplay or double-meaning jokes indicate Phase 5). Use age expectations to interpret whether a child's humour corresponds to developmental norms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coding categories used in this study (Incongruity and subcategories)
rubrics_metrics.description: General categories of drawings in terms of humour were organized under 'Incongruity' with subcategories: Humorous gestures; Incongruous/strange behaviours (animals/people); Objects/distortion (corrupting/transfer of characteristics); Incongruous appearance (colour, size, shape); The naming of objects/events/people in an incongruous way (naming inaccurately); Misfortunes/clumsiness or misbehaviours.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply these concrete subcategories when coding drawings and associated explanations. The paper gives explicit examples for each (e.g., sticking out tongue → humorous gesture; human face on an animal → transfer of characteristics; dropped ice cream → misfortune). A child may produce multiple items (codes) per drawing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Drawing technique as a nonverbal data collection method
rubrics_metrics.description: Drawing is described as a nonverbal technique that 'opens a window' to children's opinions and emotions and reveals images in the child's mind; the quality and content of drawings reveal children's perceptions of self and others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use drawing to elicit representations children may not verbalize. Provide plain A4 paper and pastels/crayons of all colors; ask the child to draw the person/object/event that makes them laugh; follow up with an interview so the child's intent and meaning are recorded (drawings alone are ambiguous).

rubrics_metrics.name: Semi-structured interview procedure with preschoolers
rubrics_metrics.description: Researcher introduced herself with the class teacher, interviewed each child alone in another classroom, asked what makes him/her laugh most and who is the funniest person, and encouraged answers. After drawing, the researcher interviewed the child face-to-face and wrote down what the child said.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One-on-one semi-structured interviews both before (to prompt memory) and after drawing (to elicit explanation/validation) are recommended. Encourage but do not lead responses; record verbatim child explanations to increase validity of interpreting drawings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sampling criteria for preschool humour studies (purposive / convenience)
rubrics_metrics.description: The study used purposive sampling (convenience sample) with a designated criterion: children aged 5–6 years; participants were voluntary and showing normal development; preschools were public independent preschools attached to the Ministry of National Education.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select children purposefully to obtain rich, in-depth information (criterion sampling for a specific age/stage). Rationale given: 5–6 year-olds are at the pre-schema period and are eager to talk about drawings and aware that drawings represent feelings/thoughts. Report recruitment context and inclusion criteria (voluntary, typical development).

rubrics_metrics.name: Content analysis approach for qualitative drawing and interview data
rubrics_metrics.description: Content analysis steps: obtaining data through interview, observation and documents; coding of data; finding themes; organizing the codes and themes; defining the findings and interpreting them. In this study codes and themes were 'composed directly, which were not determined before' (inductive).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use inductive content analysis: prepare notes and transcripts, perform open coding, group codes into themes, and interpret findings in light of theory (Absurd, McGhee, Bariaud). Document the coding process and decisions to support credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Validity and reliability procedures: triangulation and inter-coder agreement
rubrics_metrics.description: Validity and reliability were obtained via triangulation techniques, specifically researcher triangulation: more than one researcher participated in data collection and analysis; two researchers coded separately; a third researcher reviewed analyses and discussions resolved incompatible codes. Reliability was estimated using the formula: Reliability = Consensus / (Consensus + Disagreement) x 100.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implement multiple coders, independent coding, and third-party adjudication to increase trustworthiness. Compute inter-coder reliability with the provided consensus formula and document how discordances were resolved.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical data-collection logistics during drawing sessions
rubrics_metrics.description: Each child was taken to another room, given a sheet of A4 paper and pastels of every color, and told to draw; while drawing the researcher kept notes and recorded the figures; after drawing the child was interviewed and the researcher wrote what the child said.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure a quiet private space, provide unrestricted drawing materials, take observational notes during the drawing process, photograph or save drawings, and capture the child's verbal account immediately after drawing for accurate linkage between image and meaning.
